title: Design-Gate Sequences
blurb: Three sequences a system passes through before it ever touches a real user — put each one in order.
source: AIGP BOK III.A · AIGP Study Guide (SG) §Domain III.A · scored backup in G10 (The Development Desk) and the risk-treatment/risk-controls/risk-hierarchy-pairs decks

ladders.title: Idea → Pilot
ladders.prompt: Order the gates a new AI system passes through from first business case to shadow-mode readiness evidence.

steps.label: Business case & objectives
steps.detail: Define why AI at all: the cost-benefit case, including societal impacts, comes first. Nothing downstream can be evaluated without a stated objective to measure it against.

steps.label: Use case + impact assessment (leveraged from a PIA)
steps.detail: Scope the specific use case and run an impact assessment to anticipate and manage the harms it could cause. The best existing template to adapt is a privacy impact assessment (PIA/DPIA) — governance doesn't invent this from scratch.

steps.label: Design — risk-impact estimation & architecture
steps.detail: Design work includes estimating risk impact and choosing architecture. This is the first gate where architecture is actually decided; planning explicitly excludes it — planning sets objectives and governance approach, design picks how the system is built (; planning excludes architecture, ).

steps.label: Build
steps.detail: Construct the system against the design's risk-impact estimate and chosen architecture.

steps.label: Benchmark vs human experts in the same decision context
steps.detail: Before piloting, compare the system's performance against human expert performance in the same domain — this is the most valuable governance benchmark, not an abstract accuracy target.

steps.label: Pilot — validate fairness + accuracy at controlled scale
steps.detail: Run a pre-deployment pilot whose primary purpose is validating fairness and accuracy on real-world data at a controlled, limited scale before full rollout.

steps.label: Shadow-mode run as documented readiness evidence
steps.detail: Run the system in parallel with the live process (shadow mode) and document the outcomes. This documented evidence — not a verbal sign-off — is what demonstrates deployment readiness (SG-C08-Q009).

ladders.title: Mitigation hierarchy
ladders.prompt: Order the risk-mitigation hierarchy from the most durable fix to the last resort.
ladders.citation: Transparency zone backs Warn-and-train), risk-treatment.json (Accept zone backs Accept-with-monitoring), G14 Post-market monitoring zone (audit-log/post-market-review half of the final tier), risk-hierarchy-pairs.json.

steps.label: Eliminate the risk
steps.detail: Remove the risky feature or use case entirely — don't use AI in the high-risk context at all, the way a recruitment algorithm that keeps producing biased outcomes gets retired rather than endlessly patched. In the exam's parallel vocabulary this same top tier is called 'Avoid': stop undertaking the activity so the exposure goes to zero. Same concept, different label — defuse the vocabulary clash, don't pick a side.

steps.label: Substitute with a lower-risk design
steps.detail: If elimination isn't feasible, swap in a simpler, more interpretable model or a lower-risk dataset that achieves the same purpose — an opaque model for an interpretable one, a noisier dataset for one collected under stricter quality controls. Exam phrasing sometimes folds this into 'Mitigate' (act on likelihood or impact while the activity continues) — again, the same design move under a different word.

steps.label: Engineer safeguards
steps.detail: Build safeguards into the system itself: confidence thresholds, robustness testing, bias audits, explainability tools — and human-in-the-loop controls, which sit here as one example technique among several, not as a separate last-resort tier of their own. This is where most technical controls live, and where the exam's 'Mitigate/Reduce' bucket lands too.

steps.label: Warn and train users
steps.detail: Once the system itself is as safe as engineering can make it, the next line of defense is telling people: interpretability dashboards, plain-language warnings, and user training so people interacting with the system understand its limits. This is a distinct tier from engineering controls — it changes what the human knows, not what the system does.

steps.label: Accept with monitoring
steps.detail: Whatever risk remains after the four tiers above is knowingly accepted and watched — audit logs and post-market review, not silent tolerance. The exam's final tier, 'Accept', maps cleanly onto this one: a recorded decision, owned at the right level of authority, backed by ongoing monitoring rather than a one-time sign-off. Some frameworks insert Administrative controls as a distinct tier — the NIOSH-style hierarchy taught in Hierarchy of Controls — same idea, different slicing.

ladders.title: Harms-matrix workflow
ladders.prompt: Order the steps for running a probability × severity harms matrix during design.

steps.label: Enumerate harms per stakeholder
steps.detail: List the ways the system could go wrong for each affected group — end users, downstream subjects, operators — before scoring anything. Stakeholder mapping widens the lens beyond the development team so no group's exposure is missed.

steps.label: Score probability × severity
steps.detail: Rate each enumerated harm on likelihood and impact using pre-defined scales. This scoring is applied throughout design and testing, not as a one-off exercise, so new findings can move items on the grid (SG-C08-Q006).

steps.label: Prioritize — catastrophic overrides score
steps.detail: Rank by the plotted score, but let a catastrophic-impact item override a merely-average priority ranking: a low-likelihood, high-severity failure in an autonomous system still triggers a hard gate even if its raw score wouldn't top the list.

steps.label: Apply the mitigation hierarchy at the design source
steps.detail: Fix the highest-priority harms at the design/source level rather than bolting on disclaimers or monitoring after the fact — e.g. designing a chatbot's dialogue for crisis scenarios instead of relying on a disclaimer, or designing a model to exclude financially vulnerable customers from a harmful offer rather than flagging them after the fact.

steps.label: Document residual risk & owner
steps.detail: Record what risk remains after mitigation, at what score, and who is accountable for accepting it. An unrecorded residual risk is indistinguishable from an unmanaged one.
